The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The tensor factors and product pairing in the Definition are supplied by [F1]. For every $n\ge1$, [F2] makes $P_\pm^{(n)}$ an orthogonal projection. The range of an orthogonal projection is closed: if $P x_k=x_k$ and $x_k\to x$, boundedness of $P$ gives $P x=\lim_k P x_k=\lim_k x_k=x$. Therefore each $\mathcal H_\pm^{(n)}$ is a closed subspace of the complete tensor Hilbert space and is itself complete.

For $\psi,\varphi\in\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$, Cauchy–Schwarz for the square-summable nonnegative sequences $(\|\psi_n\|)_n$ and $(\|\varphi_n\|)_n$ gives
$\sum_n|\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle|\le(\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_n\|\varphi_n\|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Hence the displayed pairing converges absolutely, is sesquilinear, and is positive definite because $\langle\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2=0$ forces every coordinate to vanish.

Let $(\psi^{(k)})_k$ be Cauchy in this norm. For each fixed $n$, $(\psi_n^{(k)})_k$ is Cauchy in the complete sector $\mathcal H_\pm^{(n)}$, so it converges to some $\psi_n\in\mathcal H_\pm^{(n)}$. If $k\ge K$ and $\|\psi^{(k)}-\psi^{(m)}\|\le\varepsilon$ for all $m\ge K$, then for every finite $N$, passing $m\to\infty$ in the finite sum yields $\sum_{n\le N}\|\psi_n-\psi_n^{(k)}\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$. Also $\sum_{n\le N}\|\psi_n\|^2\le2\|\psi^{(k)}\|^2+2\varepsilon^2$. Taking suprema over finite $N$ proves $\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$, so $\psi\in\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$, and then $\|\psi^{(k)}-\psi\|\le\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Thus the direct sum is complete.

For $\psi\in\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$, truncating after sector $N$ changes its squared norm by $\sum_{n>N}\|\psi_n\|^2\to0$. Therefore the finite-particle subspace is dense and $\Omega$ is a unit vector.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $I$ be a specified finite or countably infinite
mode set with a fixed enumeration, and let $\mathfrak h=\ell^2(I)$ have its
coordinate orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in I}$. Put
$\mathfrak h^{\otimes 0}=\mathbb C$, $\mathfrak h^{\otimes 1}=\mathfrak h$,
and define each completed tensor power recursively by
$\mathfrak h^{\otimes(n+1)}=\mathfrak h^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes\mathfrak h$,
using the first-variable-linear product inner product of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. For $n\ge1$, let
$U_\pi$ permute the tensor factors for $\pi\in S_n$, and let
$$
P_\pm^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\chi_\pm(\pi)U_\pi, \qquad \chi_+(\pi)=1,\quad \chi_-(\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi),
$$
with $P_\pm^{(0)}=I_{\mathbb C}$. The permutation-sector theorem
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] makes these orthogonal
projections. Define the symmetric and antisymmetric sectors
$\mathcal H_\pm^{(n)}:=\operatorname{ran}P_\pm^{(n)}$. Define
$$
\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h):=\left\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\psi_n\in\mathcal H_\pm^{(n)},\ \sum_{n\ge0}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}, \qquad \langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\ge0}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle.
$$
The vector $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$ is the vacuum, and the finite-particle
subspace consists of vectors with only finitely many nonzero components.

This is a mathematical construction for a specified mode basis. Choosing its
symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a physical species is a separate model
postulate. No spin-statistics theorem or physical species assignment is part of
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Let $n=|m|$. In the bosonic permutation average $P_+^{(n)}x_m$, each distinct product word with occupation profile $m$ occurs $\prod_jm_j!$ times out of $n!$ permutations. Therefore $$ P_+^{(n)}x_m=\frac{\prod_jm_j!}{n!}\sum_{w\in\mathcal W(m)}w, \qquad |\mathcal W(m)|=\frac{n!}{\prod_jm_j!}. $$ The product words are orthonormal by [F1], so the squared norm of this average is $\prod_jm_j!/n!$; the prefactor in $|m\rangle_B$ makes its norm one. Distinct occupation profiles have disjoint word supports, hence their vectors are orthogonal.

If a fermionic list repeats a mode, [F2] makes its antisymmetrization zero; $\Omega_F$ excludes these profiles. For distinct occupied modes, the $n!$ permuted product words are distinct orthonormal vectors with coefficients $\pm1/n!$, so $\|P_-^{(n)}x_m\|^2=1/n!$. The prefactor $\sqrt{n!}$ normalizes the vector. Distinct occupied subsets have disjoint product-word support and are orthogonal.

The fixed enumeration identifies a finite-support configuration with a finite sequence of natural indices and finitely many nonnegative integer labels (or bits); the union over all finite sequence lengths is countable. Thus $\Omega_B$ and $\Omega_F$ are countable and their $\ell^2$ coordinate descriptions are well defined.

On the bosonic basis, shifting the coordinate index gives $\|a_jc\|^2=\sum_m m_j|c_m|^2$ and $\|a_j^\dagger c\|^2=\sum_m(m_j+1)|c_m|^2$. Hence the stated weighted domains are exactly the domains on which the shifted coefficient sequences lie in $\ell^2$. If $c^{(r)}\to c$ and either shifted sequence converges in $\ell^2$, coordinate convergence shows the limiting output has the same weighted-shift coordinates; its square summability puts $c$ in the displayed domain. Thus both maximal shifts are closed. Testing the adjoint identity against each basis vector forces the reverse weighted shift [F3], while Cauchy--Schwarz gives the converse pairing bound [F4]. Truncating to finite initial sets of configurations makes the weighted tails tend to zero in graph norm, so $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a core for both shifts under the graph definition in [F3].

Product words span a dense subspace of each tensor power by [F1]. Applying the bounded projections $P_\pm^{(n)}$ to that dense span gives a dense subspace of each projected sector. Every projected product word is either zero or a scalar multiple of the corresponding occupation vector from steps 1.1–1.2. Thus the occupation vectors are complete in each sector and, after taking the direct sum over $n$, form orthonormal bases of the Fock spaces.

For $i=j$, direct action on $|m\rangle_B$ gives $a_ja_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=(m_j+1)|m\rangle_B$ and $a_j^\dagger a_j|m\rangle_B=m_j|m\rangle_B$. For $i\ne j$, both orders of distinct coordinate shifts give the same coefficient and same occupation vector, so the shifts commute; the same direct coordinate calculation applies to two annihilators and two creators. This proves the CCR on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, without asserting that unbounded commutators are defined on all Fock space.

Each fermionic shift maps a subset of an orthonormal basis into another orthonormal subset with coefficients of modulus at most one, so it is a contraction on the finite span and extends boundedly. For distinct $i,j$, the two orders in any CAR anticommutator are either both zero or have equal magnitudes and opposite signs: toggling the earlier mode changes by one the number of occupied modes preceding the later index. For $i=j$, if $m_j=0$ then $c_jc_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=|m\rangle_F$ and $c_j^\dagger c_j|m\rangle_F=0$; if $m_j=1$ the roles reverse. The other same-mode anticommutators vanish. Thus all CAR identities hold on the basis span and extend by boundedness to the whole Fock space.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized. Define $\bar E:=\langle E\rangle_\beta$ and $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E):=\sum_i p_i(E_i-\bar E)^2$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

For $q\in(0,1)$, the bosonic geometric law on $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with weights $(1-q)q^n$ has mean $q/(1-q)$ and variance $q/(1-q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1+\mathbb E[n])$; its relative standard deviation, defined as $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E[n]$, tends to $1$ as $q\uparrow1$. The fermionic two-state law on $n\in\{0,1\}$ with weights $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$ has mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1-\mathbb E[n])$. Here Bose and Fermi name these explicitly specified counting laws; no claim about a physical preparation is made.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), with Hilbert adjoint $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

**The absolute value.** The operator $T^*T\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact, since it
is the composite of the compact $T$ with the bounded $T^*$
([[lem-compositions-with-a-compact-operator-are-compact]]); it is self-adjoint,
because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T^{**}=T^*T$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]); and it
is positive, because
$$\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\langle Tx,Tx\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\ge0$$
for every $x\in H$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]).
The **absolute value** of $T$ is the unique compact self-adjoint positive
operator
$$|T|:=(T^*T)^{1/2}$$
with $|T|^{2}=T^*T$, whose existence and uniqueness are the preceding square-root
lemma ([[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]]). It satisfies
$$\||T|x\|^{2}=\langle|T|^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\qquad(x\in H),$$
so in particular $\bigl\||T|\bigr\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]) and
$\ker|T|=\ker T$, since $\||T|x\|=\|Tx\|$ for every $x$.

**The singular values.** By the spectral theorem for $|T|$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]) the nonzero
eigenvalues of $|T|$ form a finite or countably infinite set of positive reals,
each with finite multiplicity, and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely
many of them exceed $\varepsilon$; positivity rules out negative eigenvalues and
$0$ already corresponds to the kernel. The **multiset of positive singular
values of $T$** is the multiset of positive eigenvalues of $|T|$, counted with
multiplicity ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**The ordered singular-value sequence.** The **distinct** positive singular
values are listed with positive labels in *decreasing* order $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ as follows:
if the multiset of positive eigenvalues is empty (equivalently $|T|=0$,
equivalently $T=0$), the list is empty; otherwise $\mu_1:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$
is an eigenvalue of $|T|\}$, a maximum and not merely a supremum, because a
supremum value not attained would be an accumulation point different from $0$;
having chosen $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k$, put $\mu_{k+1}:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue of $|T|$ and $\lambda<\mu_k\}$ whenever that set is nonempty, and stop
otherwise. Each step is legitimate by the finiteness-above-thresholds property
above, and an infinite list satisfies $\mu_k\to0$ (otherwise its decreasing
limit would be a nonzero accumulation point). Writing $d_k$ for the multiplicity
of $\mu_k$ (a positive integer), the **zero-padded singular-value sequence** is
$$s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3\ge\cdots$$
where $s_1=\cdots=s_{d_1}=\mu_1$, $s_{d_1+1}=\cdots=s_{d_1+d_2}=\mu_2$, and so
on; if the multiset is finite with total multiplicity $r=d_1+\cdots+d_m$, one
sets $s_n:=0$ for every $n>r$, and if $T=0$ one sets $s_n:=0$ for every
$n\ge1$. The number $s_n$ is written $s_n(T)$ and called the $n$-th **singular
value** of $T$.

**Zero-based domain and positive labels.** Set $s_0(T):=\|T\|=s_1(T)$.
Thus the numerical sequence is the function $n\mapsto s_n(T)$ on all of
$\mathbb N$, including zero. The positive-labelled tail $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$
is the multiplicity-counting list constructed above. The auxiliary initial
value $s_0$ is not an additional entry of the eigenvalue multiset, does not index
a singular vector, and is excluded from multiplicity counts and singular-value
sums, which use $n\ge1$. The full sequence satisfies
$s_0\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$ and tends to zero. This preserves the page's
positive rank labels while giving convergence statements a zero-based domain.

**Rank and the finiteness of the list.** The map $\Phi:\operatorname{ran}|T|\to\operatorname{ran}T$
given by $\Phi(|T|x):=Tx$ is well defined and linear, because $|T|x=|T|x'$ forces
$x-x'\in\ker|T|=\ker T$ and hence $Tx=Tx'$; it is injective, because $Tx=0$ gives
$x\in\ker T=\ker|T|$ and $|T|x=0$; it is surjective onto $\operatorname{ran}T$
because $T=\Phi\circ|T|$; and it is isometric, $\|Tx\|=\||T|x\|$. Hence
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}|T|$ is finite-dimensional; in that case the linear
bijection $\Phi$ gives
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T=\dim\operatorname{ran}|T|$
([[def-dimension]]). Consequently, whenever $T$ has finite rank, the positive
singular values with multiplicity number exactly
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T$, the rank of $T$, and all later $s_n$ vanish, so the
sequence is **zero-padded**. If $T$ does not have finite rank, the multiset of
positive singular values is infinite and countable
([[def-countable]]) and $s_n>0$ for every $n$, with $s_n\downarrow0$; in
particular finite rank of $T$ is characterised by the eventual vanishing $s_n=0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, and conversely such eventual vanishing forces finite rank. The sequence $(s_n)$ is numerical data only: no orthonormal system is
selected here, and the zero padding is *not* an indexing of any family of
vectors. The unordered multiset determines $(s_n)$ uniquely, so $(s_n)$ is well
defined, and $s_1(T)=\||T|\|=\|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The configuration set $\Omega_\pm$ is countable by [F1]. Every $m$ has finite support, so the sums defining $E(m)$ and $|m|$ are finite real sums. The finite-support vectors form a dense subspace of $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$.

For a finite mode set $J$, summing the positive diagonal weights independently over each bosonic coordinate gives $\prod_{j\in J}\sum_{n\ge0}q_j^n=\prod_{j\in J}(1-q_j)^{-1}$. In the fermionic case each coordinate has only two values and contributes $1+q_j$. This proves the finite-mode trace products.

For a fixed $\mu$, the countable configuration model has weights $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}$ and degeneracies one. Under the compact $\beta$-envelope in the Statement, [F2]–[F3] apply to this exact countable index set and energy $K_\mu(m)$, giving the displayed beta-derivative identities and finite moments. The envelope is stronger than trace finiteness and is stated separately.

For joint $(\beta,\mu)$ response, put $X_1(m)=E(m)$, $X_2(m)=|m|$, and natural parameter $\theta=(-\beta,\beta\mu)$. The map $(\beta,\mu)\mapsto\theta$ is a smooth bijection onto its open image for $\beta>0$, with nonzero Jacobian. The stated joint envelope is exactly the required second-moment envelope for [F5]; differentiating at fixed $\beta$ gives $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$.

Let $D_\lambda$ multiply the coordinate $c_m$ by a real number $\lambda_m$, on the domain $\sum_m\lambda_m^2|c_m|^2<\infty$. Testing the adjoint identity on each coordinate vector forces the adjoint coordinates to be $\lambda_m c_m$, so $D(D_\lambda^*)$ is exactly this weighted $\ell^2$ domain by [F8]. Conversely, on that domain Cauchy–Schwarz makes the coordinate pairing bounded and identifies the adjoint action with the same multiplier. Apply this argument to $\lambda_m=E(m)$, $|m|$, and $E(m)-\mu|m|$; all three displayed operators are self-adjoint.

Enumerate a countable mode set by increasing finite initial sets $J_M$. Their finite-support configuration sets increase to $\Omega_\pm$, so the full nonnegative trace sum is the increasing limit of the finite-mode sums. For bosons, $-\log(1-q_j)=\int_0^{q_j}(1-u)^{-1}du\le q_j/(1-q_*)$, hence $\sum_j-\log(1-q_j)<\infty$. For fermions, $\log(1+q_j)\le q_j$, hence $\sum_j\log(1+q_j)<\infty$. The products therefore have finite positive limits and equal the full diagonal trace sums; the negative fermionic gaps are finite by hypothesis, and each has finite weight.

If $\Omega_\pm$ is infinite, enumerate it as $m_1,m_2,\ldots$ and let $G_M$ retain the first $M$ diagonal entries of $G_{\beta,\mu}$; in the finite case take the full finite sum. Each $G_M$ has finite rank and hence is compact. Since the omitted entries are nonnegative and summable, their supremum is bounded by their sum, so $\|G_{\beta,\mu}-G_M\|\le\sum_{r>M}e^{-\beta(E(m_r)-\mu|m_r|)}\to0$. The norm-limit theorem therefore makes $G_{\beta,\mu}$ compact. It is positive diagonal and satisfies $G_{\beta,\mu}^*G_{\beta,\mu}=G_{\beta,\mu}^2$; uniqueness of its compact positive square root gives $|G_{\beta,\mu}|=G_{\beta,\mu}$. Its singular values are the nonnegative diagonal entries with multiplicity, whose sum is $\Xi<\infty$. Thus [F7] and the trace-class definition make it trace class and give $\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi$. Dividing by $\Xi>0$ gives a positive trace-class operator of trace one.

Fix one mode $j$, and take increasing finite mode sets $J_M$ containing it. For bosons, the trace weight of configurations in $J_M$ with occupation $n$ at $j$ is $q_j^n\prod_{i\in J_M\setminus\{j\}}(1-q_i)^{-1}$; division by the total finite trace gives $(1-q_j)q_j^n$. For fermions the same calculation gives probability $q_j^n/(1+q_j)$, for $n\in\{0,1\}$. Taking increasing limits of the nonnegative configuration sums preserves these factorizations, because every finite-support configuration is eventually included and the finite products converge by step 2.2. Factoring over any fixed finite list of modes gives the product joint law, hence independence of finite collections in this diagonal grand state.

For finite $J$, multiplying the geometric series in each bosonic coordinate gives the coefficient identity for $Z_{B,N}(J)$; multiplying the two-term polynomials in each fermionic coordinate gives the identity for $Z_{F,N}(J)$. Each coefficient sums exactly the finite canonical Boltzmann weights with total occupation $N$. For countable $I$, increasing finite mode sets increase each coefficient to its sum over all finite-support configurations; this coefficient is bounded by the finite grand trace at any admissible fugacity, and a canonical density exists exactly when the coefficient is positive. Conditioning the grand law on $|m|=N$ multiplies by the indicator of that constraint and generally couples the mode occupations.

If $0<q_j<1$, [F4] gives the stated Bose and Fermi means and variances. For a fermionic mode with $q_j\ge1$, direct summation of its two probabilities gives $\mathbb E N_j=q_j/(1+q_j)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(N_j)=q_j/(1+q_j)^2$; no geometric-series claim is used there. The bosonic bounds $\mathbb E N_j\le q_j/(1-q_*)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(N_j)\le q_j/(1-q_*)^2$, and the fermionic bounds $\mathbb E N_j\le q_j$ and $\operatorname{Var}(N_j)\le q_j$, are summable. For finite initial mode sets, independence from step 3.2 gives $\mathbb E N_M=\sum_{j\in J_M}\mathbb E N_j$ and $\mathbb E N_M^2=\sum_{j\in J_M}\operatorname{Var}(N_j)+(\sum_{j\in J_M}\mathbb E N_j)^2$. Each configuration has finite support, so $N_M\uparrow N$; passing to the increasing limits of the defining nonnegative countable sums yields finite $\mathbb E N$ and $\mathbb E N^2$, with $\operatorname{Var}(N)=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(N_j)<\infty$.

In the one-dimensional oscillator specialization, [F6] supplies the Hermite eigenbasis, energy list and exact diagonal domain; substitution of those eigenvalues into the Fock multiplier gives the stated occupation construction. This uses the actual self-adjoint oscillator carrier rather than a formal differential eigenfunction list.

For $a>0$ and an integer $r\ge0$, define $I_r(a):=\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r}e^{-ax^2}\,dx$ as the two-sided improper Riemann integral. Then

$$I_r(a)=\frac{\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)}{a^{r+1/2}},\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r+1}e^{-ax^2}\,dx=0,$$

where $\Gamma(s):=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for $s>0$. In particular, $I_0(a)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ and $I_1(a)=\sqrt\pi/(2a^{3/2})$. For every compact interval $K=[a_0,a_1]\subset(0,\infty)$, $I_r$ is continuously differentiable on $K$ and

$$I_r'(a)=-I_{r+1}(a).$$

For $s,t>0$, put $B(s,t):=\int_0^1u^{s-1}(1-u)^{t-1}\,du$. Then $B(s,t)$ is finite and

$$\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)=\Gamma(s+t)B(s,t),\qquad \Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s),\qquad \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi.$$

Consequently, if independent positive random variables have densities $x^{s-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s)$ and $x^{t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(t)$, their sum has density $x^{s+t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s+t)$.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and

$$

$$

$$0\le -\log(1-q_j)-q_j\le\frac{q_j^2}{2(1-r)},\qquad 0\le q_j-\log(1+q_j)\le\frac{q_j^2}{2}.$$
Thus the classical Maxwell–Boltzmann first-order terms have a controlled aggregate error under the stated squared-summability hypothesis.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
in the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

The exact variances are $2$ for bosons and $2/9$ for fermions, while the Poisson approximation has variance $1/2$. These are finite exact model values; since $q$ is not near zero, no small-error claim follows from this example.

Assume [[post-qsm-models-statistics-and-preparation]]. Let $\omega>0$, $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, $k_B>0$, and $T>0$; set $\epsilon=\hbar\omega$ in joules and $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$. Take the self-adjoint one-dimensional realization $H_{\rm osc}$ of $-\hbar^2(2m)^{-1}d^2/dx^2+m\omega^2x^2/2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with Hermite eigenvectors $\phi_n$, eigenvalues $\epsilon(n+1/2)$, and domain $D(H_{\rm osc})=\{\sum_nc_n\phi_n:\sum_n\epsilon^2(n+1/2)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$, as proved in [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]].
$$Z=e^{-\beta\epsilon/2}(1-e^{-\beta\epsilon})^{-1},\quad U=\epsilon(\tfrac12+\bar n),\quad \bar n=(e^{\beta\epsilon}-1)^{-1},\quad C_V=k_B(\beta\epsilon)^2\frac{e^{\beta\epsilon}}{(e^{\beta\epsilon}-1)^2}.$$
Its entropy is $S=k_B[(1+\bar n)\log(1+\bar n)-\bar n\log\bar n]$; as $T\downarrow0$, $U\to\epsilon/2$, $S,C_V\to0$. As $\beta\epsilon\downarrow0$, $U=\beta^{-1}+O(\beta\epsilon^2)$.

For a separate two-level spin model $H_s=-h\sigma_z$ with $h\in\mathbb R$ in joules, $Z_s=2\cosh(\beta h)$, $U_s=-h\tanh(\beta h)$, $C_{V,s}=k_B(\beta h)^2\operatorname{sech}^2(\beta h)$, and $S_s\to0$ as $T\downarrow0$ when $h\ne0$, whereas $S_s=k_B\log2$ when $h=0$. These results make no generic third-law claim.

derivations.claim: Since $e^{-\beta\epsilon}\to0$ as $T\downarrow0$, the oscillator formulas give $\bar n\to0$, $U=\epsilon(1/2+\bar n)\to\epsilon/2$, and the entropy function in [F1] tends zero.
With $h=0$, the spin Gibbs weights are both $1/2$, so $S=-k_B(2)(1/2)\log(1/2)=k_B\log2$ independently of $T$. Both conclusions are exact consequences of these declared Hamiltonians.

For a declared nonrelativistic quantum model, adopt a complex Hilbert space, positive trace-one states, and Born probabilities for its specified measurements. Specify the one-particle modes, Hamiltonian and interactions. When the modeled particles are assigned bosonic or fermionic statistics, choose the symmetric or antisymmetric sector, respectively, as an independent physical assumption. This selection is not derived from the Fock construction or a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

For a canonical preparation at inverse temperature $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}>0$, adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ on the declared fixed-particle-number sector only when $0<Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation with chemical potential $\mu$, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta(H-\mu N)}$ only when the corresponding trace is finite and positive, as explicitly checked for the diagonal Fock model in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Fixed-number and grand-canonical preparations are distinct assumptions; in general the latter has independent mode occupations while conditioning on fixed total number couples them.

The assignments of $U=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)$, $S=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$ and thermodynamic potentials are model definitions where their traces exist. An identification with measured macroscopic thermodynamic quantities requires a separate physical bridge. No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

Adopt the model preparation of [[post-qsm-models-statistics-and-preparation]]. Let $d\ge1$, $L,m,\hbar,k_B,T>0$, $V=L^d$, $\alpha=\hbar^2/(2m)$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and let $g\in\mathbb N$ count distinct internal modes. Define the one-particle Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d\times\{1,\ldots,g\})$ with diagonal energies $\epsilon_k=\alpha|2\pi k/L|^2$ and domain $\sum_{k,s}\epsilon_k^2|c_{k,s}|^2<\infty$. This is a spectral periodic-box model; no differential-operator realization is required.

For bosons take $\mu<0$; for fermions take any finite $\mu\in\mathbb R$. In either case the grand trace is finite, mode occupations are independent in the adopted grand state, and
$$\bar n_{k,s}=\frac1{e^{\beta(\epsilon_k-\mu)}\mp1},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N_{k,s})=\bar n_{k,s}(1\pm\bar n_{k,s}),$$
with the upper sign choice in the denominator interpreted as $-$ for bosons and $+$ for fermions (equivalently the variance is $\bar n(1+\bar n)$ for bosons and $\bar n(1-\bar n)$ for fermions). For fixed $\beta,\mu$ in these regimes, as $L\to\infty$,
$$\frac{\mathbb E N}{V}\to\frac{g}{(2\pi)^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{dp}{e^{\beta(\alpha|p|^2-\mu)}\mp1},\qquad \frac{\mathbb E H}{V}\to\frac{g}{(2\pi)^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{\alpha|p|^2\,dp}{e^{\beta(\alpha|p|^2-\mu)}\mp1}.$$
The continuum limits are conditional model deductions; they assert no thermalization or measured density.

derivations.claim: The one-particle sector has exactly the two basis states $|1,0\rangle$ and $|0,1\rangle$, with weights $w_1,w_2$. Normalization gives probabilities $p_1,p_2$ with $p_1+p_2=1$, so $\mathbb E N_i=p_i$ and $N_1N_2=0$ in every canonical state outcome.

Hence $\operatorname{Cov}(N_1,N_2)=\mathbb E(N_1N_2)-\mathbb E N_1\mathbb E N_2=-p_1p_2<0$. The grand product law in [F1] is independent instead. Thus the constraint changes the joint law, without implying any general finite-volume ensemble-equivalence failure.

Under the ideal spectral gas model of [[pthm-qsm-periodic-ideal-occupation]], specialize to $d=3$ and $\alpha=\hbar^2/(2m)>0$. For finite $\mu$ and $\beta>0$, the continuum number and energy densities are
$$\rho(\mu,\beta)=\frac{g}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3k}{e^{\beta(\alpha|k|^2-\mu)}+1},\quad u(\mu,\beta)=\frac{g}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\alpha|k|^2d^3k}{e^{\beta(\alpha|k|^2-\mu)}+1}.$$
For each $\rho>0$ and $\beta>0$ there is a unique $\mu(\rho,\beta)$ giving that density. As $\beta\to\infty$, $\mu(\rho,\beta)\to E_F$ and $u\to(3/5)\rho E_F$, where
$$k_F=(6\pi^2\rho/g)^{1/3},\qquad E_F=\alpha k_F^2.$$
The ideal grand thermodynamic pressure $p$ defined by
$$p=\frac{g}{\beta(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\log(1+e^{-\beta(\alpha|k|^2-\mu)})d^3k$$
satisfies $p=2u/3$; hence its zero-temperature endpoint is $2\rho E_F/5$.

derivations.claim: Setting $g=2$ in [F1] gives $k_F=(3\pi^2\rho)^{1/3}$ and $E_F=\alpha k_F^2=\hbar^2k_F^2/(2m)$. Dividing the energy density $u$ by the number density $\rho$ gives mean energy per particle $3E_F/5$.
The pressure identity in [F1] yields $p=(2/3)(3/5)\rho E_F=2\rho E_F/5$. The result applies to the ideal continuum model and supplies no material-specific or empirical pressure.

Adopt the homogeneous periodic Bose model of [[pthm-qsm-periodic-ideal-occupation]] with one internal mode ($g=1$), dimension $d\ge1$, $\alpha=\hbar^2/(2m)>0$, fixed $\beta>0$ and target mean number density $\rho>0$. For each $L$, choose the unique $\mu_L<0$ solving
$$L^{-d}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(e^{\beta(\alpha|2\pi k/L|^2-\mu_L)}-1)^{-1}=\rho.$$
Define $\rho_c=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}(e^{\beta\alpha|p|^2}-1)^{-1}dp$ as an extended nonnegative number. Then $\rho_c=(4\pi\beta\alpha)^{-d/2}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\ell^{-d/2}$; it is finite exactly when $d>2$. For $d\le2$, $\mathbb E N_0/L^d\to0$ for every finite $\rho$. For $d>2$, $\mathbb E N_0/L^d\to(\rho-\rho_c)_+$, where $(x)_+=\max(x,0)$. When $d=3$, $\rho_c=\lambda_T^{-3}\zeta(3/2)$, $\lambda_T=(2\pi\hbar^2\beta/m)^{1/2}$, and the positive mean condensed fraction below $T_c=[2\pi\hbar^2/(mk_B)](\rho/\zeta(3/2))^{2/3}$ is $1-(T/T_c)^{3/2}$.

If $d>2$ and $\rho_0=\rho-\rho_c>0$, the grand-state ground occupation satisfies
$$\operatorname{Var}(N_0/L^d)\to\rho_0^2,\qquad \mathbb P(N_0/L^d\ge x)\to e^{-x/\rho_0}\quad(x>0).$$
In particular the condensate density does not converge in probability to its mean limit in this grand ensemble.

derivations.claim: The linked theorem gives $\mathbb E N_0=\rho_0V+o(V)$. Substitution into the geometric variance $\bar n_0(1+\bar n_0)$ and division by $V^2$ gives limit $\rho_0^2$.

At $x=2\rho_0$, the probability of a density at least $2\rho_0$ tends $e^{-2}>0$. Every such event differs from the limiting mean density $\rho_0$ by at least $\rho_0$, so convergence in probability to $\rho_0$ is impossible. This conclusion is specific to the grand preparation; a fixed-number state has $N_0$ constrained by total number.
